topic: 1. Peaceful protest is a basic feature of democracy
note: Quote is the Court's own (para 200, in Swatanter Kumar J.'s opinion; Bench B.S. Chauhan and Swatanter Kumar JJ). The original quote stopped mid-sentence and did not contain the words supporting 'the government should respect it'; extended to the end of the next sentence. (2012) 5 SCC 1 is confirmed as the citation by the Court's own text in MKSS (2018) and Amit Sahni (2020), which cite Ramlila that way. The research note on para 81 is right: that line is respondent No.4's submission.

fix.quote: Freedom of speech, right to assemble and demonstrate by holding dharnas and peaceful agitations are the basic features of a democratic system. The people of a democratic country like ours have a right to raise their voice against the decisions and actions of the Government or even to express their resentment over the actions of the Government on any subject of social or national importance. The Government has to respect and, in fact, encourage exercise of such rights.

topic: 2. Prohibitory orders: who and how long
note: BNSS s.163(1),(3),(4) verbatim (MHA gazette PDF re-opened). Number correct (CrPC 144 equivalent). Note the extension is only 'for preventing danger to human life, health or safety or for preventing a riot or any affray', by notification; the point's 'unless the State Government extends it' is acceptable but the page could add 'in limited cases'.

topic: 2. Prohibitory orders: you can ask for one to be cancelled
note: Quote verbatim from 163(5). The point's 'or the State Government, for an extension' rests on 163(6), which the law field did not cite. Hearing right is 163(7): 'early opportunity of appearing ... and showing cause'; reasons for rejection recorded in writing.

Quote verbatim (BNS s.223, number correct, replaces IPC 188). The original point ('is itself an offence') said more than the section: s.223 makes disobedience an offence only where it causes or tends to cause the listed harm (or risk of it). Point rewritten to the section's terms; clause (b) now read and given in the note.

fix.point: Knowingly disobeying a lawful prohibitory order is an offence where the disobedience causes, or tends to cause, obstruction, annoyance or injury (or the risk of it) to anyone lawfully employed: up to six months' simple imprisonment or a fine of up to Rs 2,500. Where it causes or tends to cause danger to life, health or safety, or a riot or affray, it is up to one year or a fine of up to Rs 5,000. The person need not intend harm; it is enough to know of the order.
fix.note: Clause (b) and the Explanation read from the gazette (page 62): '(b) and where such disobedience causes or tends to cause danger to human life, health or safety, or causes or tends to cause a riot or affray, shall be punished with imprisonment of either description for a term which may extend to one year, or with fine which may extend to five thousand rupees, or with both. Explanation.—It is not necessary that the offender should intend to produce harm ... It is sufficient that he knows of the order which he disobeys, and that his disobedience produces, or is likely to produce, harm.'

topic: 2. Supreme Court tests for prohibitory orders
note: Court's own summary (para 140, 'Before parting we summarise the legal position'), not a submission. Every segment verbatim apart from Indian Kanoon page numbers (117, 118) and a stray space before commas in the source. The point's 'are for emergencies' had no support in the quote; item (i) added, which also says the power covers apprehended, not only present, danger. AIR 2020 SC 1308 shown on the page; (2020) 3 SCC 637 is not shown anywhere in the opened copy and stays unverified.

fix.quote: i. ... However, the danger contemplated should be in the nature of an “emergency” and for the purpose of preventing obstruction and annoyance or injury to any person lawfully employed. ii. The power under Section 144, Cr.P.C cannot be used to suppress legitimate expression of opinion or grievance or exercise of any democratic rights. iii. An order passed under Section 144, Cr.P.C. should state the material facts to enable judicial review of the same. ... iv. While exercising the power under Section 144, Cr.P.C. the Magistrate is duty bound to balance the rights and restrictions based on the principles of proportionality and thereafter apply the least intrusive measure. v. Repetitive orders under Section 144, Cr.P.C. would be an abuse of power.

fix.law: In re Ramlila Maidan Incident, Supreme Court, 23 February 2012, para 44 (Swatanter Kumar J.); (2012) 5 SCC 1

note: BNS s.189(1) and Explanation verbatim; number correct (IPC 141). 189(1)(a) is 'to overawe by criminal force, or show of criminal force', which is intimidation, not 'using criminal force against'; point reworded to the section.

fix.point: A gathering of five or more people is an 'unlawful assembly' only if their shared aim is one of a few listed things: to intimidate the government, a legislature or a public servant by criminal force or a show of it; to resist the carrying out of a law or legal process; to commit mischief, criminal trespass or another offence; or to use criminal force to take property or force someone to act against their rights. A gathering that starts lawful can become unlawful later.

topic: 4. Protest areas cannot simply be banned
note: The quoted paras 69-70 are the Court's own but concern only the Boat Club area and the s.144 orders; Jantar Mantar (an NGT ban) is dealt with in paras 61-65 ('the solution was not to ban the demonstrations altogether', para 63; guidelines and prior permission, para 65). The original point attributed a holding on 'Jantar Mantar and the Boat Club' to paras 69-70 and said 'not allowed', which the Court did not say; it also allowed only 'very restrictive and limited use' of the Boat Club. The source break inside para 69 is a running header ('Writ Petition (Civil) No. 1153 of 2017 & Ors. Page 69 of 72'), not only a page marker. (2018) 17 SCC 324 is confirmed by Amit Sahni (2020) citing MKSS that way.

fix.point: The Supreme Court held that the authorities should regulate protests at Jantar Mantar and at the Boat Club in Delhi rather than ban them altogether. It said the repeated prohibitory orders at the Boat Club amounted in practice to a ban, and directed the Delhi Police to frame guidelines, including prior permission, for limited use of both places.
fix.law: Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan v. Union of India, Supreme Court, 23 July 2018, paras 63-65 (Jantar Mantar) and 69-70 (Boat Club); AIR 2018 SC 3476; (2018) 17 SCC 324
fix.quote: Though this analysis of the NGT is without blemish, we, however, feel that the solution was not to ban the demonstrations altogether. ... However, in reality no such activities are allowed at all and, therefore, the situation which is created amounts to ‘banning’ these public meetings, demonstrations, dharnas, etc. altogether rather than ‘regulating’ the same. 70) In the aforesaid conspectus, here also the Commissioner of Police, New Delhi and other official respondents can frame proper guidelines for regulating such protests, demonstrations, etc.

note: The original quote is the Additional Solicitors General's argument for the Delhi Police (para 24), a party's submission. Replaced with the Court's own reading of the same orders (para 68). The original point named 'state police Acts', which no opened source supports; removed.

fix.point: Whether you need police permission, and where you may protest, is set locally, for example by police orders in a city, and differs from place to place. Check with the local police station or a lawyer before the day.
fix.quote: The reading of these orders, thus, would indicate that there is no absolute prohibition from holding public meetings, processions, demonstrations, etc. Such activities are to be restricted in larger public interest and, therefore, before any group of persons or person wants to carry out any such processions and dharnas, it has to take prior written permission.
fix.law: Example: the Delhi Police prohibitory orders, as read by the Supreme Court in Mazdoor Kisan Shakti Sangathan v. Union of India (2018), para 68

topic: 5. Notice to appear instead of arrest
note: Quote verbatim (35(3) has a 'sub-section ( 1)' spacing artefact). The original point's 'For offences punishable with up to seven years' is not in 35(3), which applies 'in all cases where the arrest of a person is not required under sub-section (1)'; the seven-year line belongs to 35(1)(b). Point rewritten to the text and given the 35(4) duty and 35(6) consequence, which a lay reader needs.

fix.point: If the police do not need to arrest you, they must instead give you a notice to appear before them, and you must comply with it. If you comply, you should not be arrested for that offence unless the officer records reasons. If you do not comply, or will not identify yourself, you can be arrested.

note: BNSS s.53(1) verbatim; number correct (CrPC 54). The second proviso (a woman examined by or under a female medical officer) begins on the next gazette page and was not extracted, as noted.

topic: 6. Women: no arrest at night, save exceptionally
note: Quote verbatim; number correct (CrPC 46(4)). The original point said 'written permission'; the section requires a written report to obtain prior permission and does not say the permission is in writing.

fix.point: A woman should not be arrested after sunset and before sunrise, except in exceptional circumstances. In such a case a woman police officer must first make a written report and get the permission of a first-class Magistrate.

topic: 6. Women: not to be touched by a male officer
note: Quote verbatim (43(1) proviso); s.49(2) read in the gazette and the note's text is exact. Original point dropped 'unless the circumstances indicate to the contrary' and stated 'Only a woman may search a woman' more broadly than 49(2)'s wording; both tightened. The note's finding that no BNSS provision requires a woman officer 'where practicable' is consistent with ss.43 and 49 as read.

fix.point: When a woman is arrested, she is presumed to submit to custody once told orally of the arrest, unless the circumstances suggest otherwise, and a male officer should not touch her to make the arrest unless the circumstances require it. When a woman has to be searched, the search must be made by another woman, with strict regard to decency.

note: Art 39A verbatim. It is a Directive Principle, as noted; 'any citizen' in the text.

Quote verbatim from NALSA's copy (PDF re-opened, 200, same size). The original point ('Anyone in custody is entitled') omitted s.12's condition that the person 'has to file or defend a case' and s.13(1)'s prima facie test, so it said more than the Act. 12(h) amounts (Rs 9,000 / Rs 12,000 'or such other higher amount as may be prescribed') are in the text; current state limits were not checked.

fix.point: If you have a case to bring or defend, you are entitled to free legal services if you are in custody, a woman or a child, a member of a Scheduled Caste or Scheduled Tribe, a person with a disability, a victim of trafficking, or of a disaster, ethnic violence or caste atrocity, an industrial worker, or earning below an income limit set by your state. The legal services authority must be satisfied you have a prima facie case; a sworn statement of your income is normally enough.
fix.law: Legal Services Authorities Act, 1987, sections 12 and 13
